title: AuroraJobs
scope: The whole application: the student product, the employer portal, the internal dashboard, deployments, and infrastructure.
summary: Jobs and careers platform for university students, employers, and university career services. I was responsible for the application end to end, in a Ruby on Rails monolith.
problemLine: Students looking for a first job and companies hiring junior profiles don't find each other on general job boards.
context: Students looking for a first job and companies hiring junior profiles rarely meet somewhere built for that stage: general job boards treat both as one more case. AuroraJobs put jobs, training, and content around that specific moment.
audience: University students taking their first steps, companies hiring junior profiles, and university career services.

responsibility.summary: The application was mine end to end: data modelling, backend, frontend, testing, deployments, and infrastructure. I joined with little experience and the CTO coached me until I could make those calls on my own.

fronts.title: The student product
fronts.description: Profiles, dynamic filters and forms for describing what they were after, job listings, and the full application flow.

fronts.title: The employer product
fronts.description: Panels showing each opening's candidates already ranked, with their video interview and the reject, save, or contact actions on the same screen.

fronts.title: The internal dashboard
fronts.description: The tool the team used to configure all of the above — filters, forms, and ranking criteria — without going through a deployment.

inventory: Matching engine between students and openings.
Analytics dashboards for university career services.

responsibility.teamBoundary: Product made the final call. I took part in shaping ideas, argued about scope, and proposed simpler alternatives when I saw one. I mentored, coordinated, and managed a team of two developers, one junior and one mid: splitting the work, reviewing it, and supporting them day to day.

decisions.title: A Rails monolith instead of services
decisions.situation: There were few of us, and profiles, openings, matching, applications, content, and analytics all had to be built at roughly the same time.
decisions.decision: Keep everything in a Ruby on Rails monolith, with Sidekiq for async work.
decisions.rationale: At that team size, splitting into services would have added deployments, contracts between parts, and scattered debugging without solving any problem we actually had.
decisions.change: Data model and interface changed together, and a complete feature fit into a short cycle.

decisions.title: Make configurable whatever changed every week
decisions.situation: Filters, student forms, and ranking criteria shifted with every product conversation. Each tweak was a development task and a deployment.
decisions.decision: Move them into the internal dashboard and let the team configure them there.
decisions.rationale: What changes for business reasons should not have to go through me to change.
decisions.change: Product adjusted filters and forms without waiting on development, and I stopped receiving tickets that were business decisions dressed as technical work.

decisions.title: Split the work and review it instead of building it all
decisions.situation: The product was growing faster than I could write it, and two developers joined the team.
decisions.decision: Split work by area, review their pull requests, and pair when it helped, rather than keeping the hard parts for myself.
decisions.rationale: Hoarding the difficult work meant the team never learned the domain and I became the bottleneck.
decisions.change: A junior and a mid owning their own areas, and architecture decisions argued in review rather than inherited.

results.statement: A live product with a job board, an employer area, careers guidance, content, and analytics.
results.evidence: The screenshots on this page are from the public product.
